title: Goose: epoll loops, own Postgres client, 5-lane bcrypt
body:
Goose entry for the multicore server challenge: epoll event loops, a hand-written Postgres client, and 5-lane bcrypt. Details are in `submissions/goose-epoll-xeonfx/README.md`.

## Latest change: batched list reads

Ported from #7 `rust-tokio-Scooter1337`, so Postgres does less work per request:
- **Batched list reads.** List reads of one kind (all, tag, author, favorited) that queue while a batch is in flight go to Postgres as one statement: parameters as arrays through `unnest(...) WITH ORDINALITY`, each member's page in a `LATERAL`, rows routed back by member number. A quiet server sends reads at once. The feed is never batched.
- **Articles read once.** When at least half the members ask for the same page, each article's tags, favorite count and author are read once per batch; `favorited` and `following` stay per member.
- **`GET /api/tags`** reads waiting together share one execution.
- **SQL.** Global and tag lists read favorite count and `favorited` in one scan of the favorites; the favorited list and comments read the viewer's favorites and followees once; creating an article inserts only missing tags.
- New settings: `READ_BATCH` (32; 0 turns batching off) and `READ_HOLD` (1).

## How it was checked

- All 197 conformance steps pass.
- A concurrent check sends the same 6,000 list and tags reads to a batched server and to one with `READ_BATCH=0` on the same database: no answer differs, and every batch form runs. With the row routing broken on purpose, 253 answers differ.

## Results (c4-highcpu-8, fresh full seed, 60 s ramp, 60 s measured, load from two c4-highcpu-8)

| Users | Build | req/s | p95 ms | p99 ms | Errors | CPU app / Postgres | Verdict |
|--:|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|---|
| 120,000 | before | 31,841 | 6.1 | 11.8 | 0 | 18% / 76% | pass |
| 120,000 | now | 31,770 | 3.7 | 6.7 | 0 | 18% / 72% | pass |
| 130,000 | before | 34,052 | 177 | 240 | 0 | 18% / 80% | pass |
| 130,000 | now | 34,486 | 6.0 | 9.8 | 0 | 19% / 75% | pass |
| 140,000 | before | 34,143 | 623 | 742 | 0 | 19% / 80% | fails p95 |
| 140,000 | now | 36,996 | 10.1 | 21.2 | 0 | 19% / 77% | pass |
| 150,000 | before | 34,074 | 951 | 1,076 | 0 | 20% / 79% | fails p95, p99 |
| 150,000 | now | 39,653 | 20.3 | 55.6 | 0 | 20% / 77% | pass |
| 160,000 | now | 41,249 | 368 | 501 | 0 | 22% / 77% | pass |
| 175,000 | now | 41,500 | 967 | 2,818 | 0 | 23% / 76% | fails p95, p99 |

Not tested before merge: 5-minute holds of the new build, and the scored run's warm-up on a database that has grown.

title: Add Kotlin/Vert.x submission
body:
## Kotlin + Vert.x (`kotlin-vertx-canleon`)

**Front: direct** · Kotlin 2.4 · Vert.x Web 5.2 · Vert.x PostgreSQL client 5.2 · JDK 27

### Goal

A fast server that is still written like a normal production service: DDD layering (domain / application /
infrastructure), standard libraries, readable code. No benchmark-only tricks: no caching, every login runs bcrypt,
every request checks the token and reads Postgres, no hand-rolled bcrypt, JWT or byte-level JSON. Every optimization
was measured; ideas without a measurable gain were dropped.

### Results

Measured locally (app + Postgres on 8 shared cores, full seed, warm-up before each run), next to `examples/java`
(behind Nginx, as its README says) on the same machine:

| | This submission | Java example |
|---|---:|---:|
| Most users that passed | 19,000 | 4,500 |
| Requests per second at that load | 16,900 | 5,900 |
| CPU per request at that load | 0.46 ms | 1.06 ms |
| p95 at 6,000 users | 4 ms | 542 ms (fails) |

About **4× the users at less than half the CPU per request**. The absolute numbers are from my machine, not the box.

### Stack and why

| | | Why |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP | Vert.x Web 5.2 with Kotlin coroutines, on Netty (native epoll) | One HTTP server per core, each with its own database connections on the same event loop: a request never changes thread. 35% less app CPU than Ktor on the same code |
| Database | Vert.x PostgreSQL client, plain SQL | Non-blocking and pipelined: 16 connections serve all requests. 12% less CPU per request than JDBC + HikariCP (25% less in Postgres); jasync-sql needed about 30% more |
| JSON | kotlinx.serialization | Compile-time serializers, no reflection |
| Auth | java-jwt (HS256) in a small route handler | One token parse per request |
| bcrypt | Bouncy Castle, cost 10 | Fastest Java implementation measured |

### Main optimizations

- **No Nginx:** the server takes the connections itself on `0.0.0.0:80` (about 29% more requests per second).
- **One SQL statement per request**, list pages pick their ids first, and each connection reuses its query plans
  (17% less Postgres CPU).
- **bcrypt on its own thread pool**, so a burst of logins can't starve Postgres. Fixed 2 GB heap.

### Checks

- Conformance suite passes (197/197) on a clean build of the commit: `install.sh` as root, `build.sh` as a normal
  user, `start.sh` in the foreground.
- All versions pinned. 16 Postgres connections on the box (capped at 90).
- One documented deviation from SPEC.md: creating an article isn't one transaction (details in the README).

title: Add go-epoll-o7livetype submission (Front: direct)
body:
**Front: direct**

## Summary

A Go Conduit server tuned for the most users per core. It serves port 80 directly from its own epoll loops
and pushes the same database design as the fasthttp submission further (pipelining, an allocation-free request
path, a faster bcrypt).

It is the benchmaxxed version of `go-fasthttp-o7livetype` until I got annoyed with go as go isn't really designed for this level of fiddley tuning like the systems level languages of C or Rust.

| Server | Front | HTTP | Database access | 1 core | 8 cores | req/s (8 cores) | vs `examples/go` (1 / 8 cores) | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `examples/go` | nginx | `net/http` | 80 pooled connections, up to 5 statements per request | 5,000 | 37,500 | 9,525 | 1.0x / 1.0x |  |
| `go-fasthttp-o7livetype` | nginx | fasthttp | 22 connections, batched, group commit, 1 statement per endpoint | 10,000 | 67,500 | 17,780 | 2.0x / 1.8x |  |
| `go-epoll-o7livetype` | direct | own epoll loops | same as fasthttp, plus pipelining and custom bcrypt | 18,500 | 135,000 | 33,645 | 3.7x / 3.6x | **<-- This submission** |

**Detailed results** (req/s, latency, CPU and memory at the 8-core limit; the multiplier is req/s against `examples/go`):

| Implementation | Front | 1 core | 8 cores | req/s | vs `examples/go` | p50 | p95 | p99 | CPU server / PG / Nginx | Memory server / Nginx / PG | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `examples/go` | nginx | 5,000 | 37,500 | 9,525 | 1.0x | 142 ms | 319 ms | 372 ms | 2.3 / 4.1 / 1.4 | 182 MB / 316 MB / 610 MB |  |
| `go-fasthttp-o7livetype` | nginx | 10,000 | 67,500 | 17,780 | 1.9x | 13 ms | 49 ms | 77 ms | 2.1 / 3.7 / 2.0 | 142 MB / 318 MB / 159 MB |  |
| `go-fasthttp-o7livetype`, no Nginx | direct | 13,500 | 100,000 | 25,818 | 2.7x | 33 ms | 318 ms | 360 ms | 3.2 / 4.7 / - | 2.0 GB / - / 159 MB |  |
| `go-epoll-o7livetype` | direct | 18,500 | 135,000 | 33,645 | 3.5x | 231 ms | 386 ms | 452 ms | 1.9 / 6.1 / - | 1.3 GB / - / 159 MB | **<-- This submission** |

Users = highest count passing the challenge's rule (p95 < 500 ms, p99 < 1 s, < 1% errors) in 1-minute runs on my
machine, not the official box; 1 core with 2 GB and 8 cores with 16 GB shared with PostgreSQL. Full results,
CPU, memory and the reasoning for each change are in the README.

## Checklist

- [x] Top 10 but I doubt it.

## Testing

- Conformance suite on dev and full seed; clean Ubuntu 24.04 install and build as a normal user
- Load-tested with `bench/cmd/loadgen` at 1 and 8 cores
- PostgreSQL stopped for 10 s under traffic: no errors, a write sent mid-outage committed exactly once
- Write batches poisoned with foreign-key violations: every valid write committed once, each bad one failed alone
- Unit and race tests for the reactor, JSON escaping, JWT and bcrypt equivalence (kept out of the submission)

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: submission: rust-urus-markk116
body:
# Hello!

Thanks for organising this nice challenge! I like the videos a lot, and I think this is a fun opportunity to showcase a project I've been working on. I write PHP for my day job, so this is a good way to let off some associative-array-induced steam.

I quite like the programming model of Erlang/Elixir/Gleam, but I don't like that these languages are kind of slow. So I've been trying to build the BEAM (Erlang's VM) in Rust, to the best of my ability. Not literally a VM, but the programming model of working with actors. So it's actually more of an alternative to Tokio, one that lets you do away with the function coloring that comes from the async/await approach to concurrency that's so popular right now. The goal is to be able to write simple, synchronous-looking code that is as performant as Tokio. I also quite like the gen_server concept from OTP, so that's in there too.

This is definitely still pretty far from a v1.0 release, but this challenge did help me find another bug, so that's a step in the right direction.

I did try to benchmark this on my desktop, with some VMs set up with proper resource limits, and I'm actually pretty positive about how it performed there (no spoilers! :P). But we'll see how it does in the real test (I hope).

I tried to keep this mostly to normal-ish code, rather than the kind of hyper-optimized stuff that was submitted to the previous challenge. Stuff you'd never deploy irl, haha. But I am also working on an "optimized to the nines" version, which I'll submit if you tell me it's okay to submit multiple entries.

In any case, I hope you find this submission interesting, and I hope I beat Pony, whose existence I only just learned about from the other submission, and whose philosophy seems pretty similar.

Kind regards,
Mark

title: Pony / Stallion / New Database Driver
body:
# Thanks

As a Pony developer, this project has been exceedingly helpful to me.  The project has spent the last 6+ months revamping and rebuilding many of our libraries as we march to Pony v1.0.0.

You provided a real use-case, and critically - built a testing / performance environment with examples from other languages to measure against.  This is gold.

With humble thanks to the Ponylang community who helped me squeeze out more performance in this design.

In my test environment, we beat all the (provided) examples by more than 30%.  Here's hoping that reflects when it hits the "real"™ hardware.

# The Language (Provided for your ease)

Pony is an actor-based language that is designed to be correct and fast. It's main selling point is that it provides a way to safely share data between actors *without* copying, or using locks or semaphores, or other blocking operations. This is all enforced in the compiler - so no "data access" checking happens at runtime. Why? Speed!

Pony actors can't exit themselves and are not allowed to crash, so we never need to check if an actor exists before sending. Why? Speed!

Pony actors don't do synchronous messaging (think Elixir's GenServer.call). Why? synchronous operations are latency. Latency is slow. Speed!

# The Design

As I've mentioned a few times, Latency is the enemy of speed. We need to reduce the number of actors between the user and the data.  Here is our design:

![Connection and database worker architecture](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/contact-red/multicore-server-challenge/refs/heads/feat/pony-stallion-no-stdlib/submissions/pony-stallion-contact-red/connection-architecture.svg)

At startup we create X number of Database Workers, where X is the number of CPUs.  These are going to be the busiest actors in our system. Remember that actors serialize, and serialization is latency and latency kills speed.

If our number of database workers is less than the number of CPUs, we're leaving CPU on the table. Any more is a waste as you can only run X number of actors at an instant in time.

Each Database Actor makes (95/X)ish™ database connections per SPEC.md

A user hits the listener. The listener creates a new Client Connection per user.

On creation, the Client Connection actor is told about a single Database Worker and uses it for all its queries.

A query comes in, the database actor knows the State (Connecting / Authenticating / Idle / Busy etc…) for each connection it is responsible for, so immediately farms the query out right to an idle connection if available.  If all database connections are busy, it queues it.

If a database worker loses a connection, or has a connection error out - it disconnects it and reconnects it.

title: Add a C# submission on minimal APIs and EF Core
body:
Adds `submissions/csharp-efcore-xeonfx/`: Conduit written the plain way in C#. Front: direct.

It uses ASP.NET Core minimal APIs, EF Core with LINQ, the standard JWT bearer handler and BCrypt.Net-Next on .NET 10. It is written to be short and easy to read, not fast. There is no raw SQL. Each response is a LINQ projection that EF Core loads in one query.

A companion to the fast version in #8, to show the distance between the plain way and a tuned one on the same box.

## Results

8-vCPU `c4-highcpu-8` set up with `box/setup-box.sh`, full seed, the load generator on a second `c4-highcpu-8`, think-scale 1, a 3-minute warm-up, then 60 s ramp + 60 s measured per probe.

| 8,000 | 17 ms | 46 ms | 0% | 75% | pass |
| 12,000 | 89 to 915 ms over 7 probes | 210 to 1,230 ms | under 0.1% | 95% | 6 of 7 passed |
| 13,000 | 661 ms | 893 ms | 0.39% | 96% | fail |

## Testing

title: Add Elixir submission using raw TCP and Postgrex
body:
Adds `submissions/elixir-raw-foovoo/`, a direct HTTP server built on `:gen_tcp`, Postgrex and `bcrypt_elixir`, with one BEAM process per keep-alive connection. Responses use iodata and named prepared SQL; writes commit before responding. JWT HS256 and expiry are checked per request, bcrypt stays at cost 10, and query results are not cached between requests.

The final source enforces a cumulative 16 KiB request-head limit across fragmented input, initializes the shared database-outage log limiter at startup, batches feed-page tag enrichment while preserving exact favorite counts and viewer checks, and skips hibernation when partial or queued input is present. Postgrex remains the sole driver. The submission contains only its source, tests, pinned dependencies/toolchains, executable install/build/start scripts and README; Rust and laboratory infrastructure are excluded.

### Validation

- Final source: **19 unit tests passed** and official conformance **197/197 on both development and full seeds**.
- Feed rewrite: **16 result/order equivalence checks**, with the other 25 SQL statements and names unchanged.
- Native build and frozen source hashes were verified; no experimental adapters, profiling or pool sharding are included.

### Local five-minute capacity probes

Local M1 Pro / Ubuntu 24.04 arm64 VM, PostgreSQL 18, full seed of 500k articles and 100k users. Server and PostgreSQL share four CPUs; four healthy Linux load generators share six separate CPUs over loopback. Each point starts with a fresh database clone and warmup, then a 60-second ramp, nominal 300-second measurement and 15-second tail.

Explicit tested profile: `POOL=8 SCHEDULERS=3:3 DIRTY_CPU=1 HIB_WORDS=2048 ERL_AFLAGS='+IOs true'`; general runtime defaults remain unchanged.

| Concurrent users | Successful req/s | p95 / p99 ms | Errors | Result |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 33,000 | 8,229.92 | 443.135 / 496.383 | 0 | PASS |
| 33,000, fresh confirmation | 8,103.53 | 474.111 / 527.359 | 0 | PASS |
| 34,000 | 8,104.07 | 660.991 / 702.975 | 0 | FAIL |
| 36,000 | 8,104.10 | 892.927 / 934.911 | 0 | FAIL |
| 40,000 | 7,944.87 | 1,595.391 / 1,647.615 | 0 | FAIL |

**33k is the confirmed highest passing tested point, bracketed by 34k failing**, under p95 < 500 ms, p99 < 1,000 ms and errors < 1%. A separate 64k probe failed with 12.54% errors, primarily HTTP503 checkout-queue drops; transaction checkout exceptions also surfaced as HTTP500.

The 33k confirmation has only 25.889 ms p95 margin and rising late latency, so this is not a claim of indefinite sustainable capacity. VM wall-clock corrections limit throughput precision: native RPS uses the nominal duration, while request latencies use monotonic timing; exact scored monotonic duration was not recorded. These local four-core ARM results are not an official eight-core x86_64 challenge score. The README records the tuning experiments, tradeoffs and limits.

title: Add Rust submission using mio and pipelined Postgres
body:
Adds `submissions/rust-mio-foovoo/`: a Rust server using raw threads, mio/epoll and a hand-written pipelined Postgres client. `Front: direct`.

On the eight-core scoring box, defaults select two event loops and eight Postgres connections. Reads share a pool routed by estimated queued work; writes use shared-Sync group commit, and every response waits for its commit. Interleaved bcrypt runs at cost 10 on background workers. JWT HS256 signatures and expiry are checked per request. The README documents dependencies, optimizations, configuration and limitations.

Only the submission folder is changed, including its pinned lockfile, executable install/build/start scripts and build-output `.gitignore`.

### Existing local validation

No new tests were run for PR preparation. The submitted implementation matches the source used for the final FEED-w1 checks; subsequent changes are documentation only.

- Local macOS arm64: debug and release `cargo test --locked` each passed 22 tests (one SQL-dump helper ignored and separately run successfully).
- Ubuntu 24.04 arm64 VM on the M1 Pro: official `test/run.sh submissions/rust-mio-foovoo`, 197/197 passed on each seed (`conduit_dev` and full `conduit_seed`), with defaults after the final FEED-only rewrite.
- Concurrency/fault-injection checks and both-seed conformance with count routing and batching disabled passed before that rewrite. The FEED change has separate equality (1,988 cases), CPU and generic-plan evidence.

### Local M1 Pro performance

MacBook Pro M1 Pro (10 cores, 32 GB), Lima Ubuntu 24.04 arm64 VM (10 vCPUs, 16 GB), PostgreSQL 18, full seed (500k articles, 100k users). The local harness restricted server plus Postgres to vCPUs 0-3 and four load-generator processes to vCPUs 4-9, using separate loopback addresses. That CPU split was local experiment setup; the submission performs no pinning.

Each probe used 60 s ramp + 60 s measured + 15 s tail:

| Revision / run | Users | req/s | p50 / p95 / p99 (ms) | Errors | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| v4 before FEED w1 (r14, top of ladder) | 80,000 | 19,645.6 | 311.0 / 453.9 / 505.9 | 0% | PASS |
| Final FEED w1 (r16-w1, short regression probe) | 76,000 | 20,140.5 | 1.8 / 9.4 / 22.6 | 0% | PASS |

Both reported `lg_limited: no` and `behind=false`. The 76k probe used the submitted implementation; the 80k result predates the FEED-only rewrite. Different host conditions mean the latency difference cannot be attributed to w1. Neither run included a five-minute hold or established a failing upper bound; these are local measurements, not an official challenge score or an eight-core x86_64 benchmark.

title: C + io_uring, no framework (c-iouring-tigokraft)
body:
Adds `submissions/c-iouring-tigokraft/`: the Conduit API in C on io_uring, with a hand-written pipelined Postgres wire client. **Front: direct.**

## What it is
- Event loops on io_uring (multishot accept, multishot readiness poll + `recv()`). Idle keep-alive connections own no buffer, about 200 bytes each.
- A Postgres v3 protocol client with SCRAM-SHA-256 and every statement prepared once per connection. Each request is one pipelined batch with one Sync. The response waits for that batch's ReadyForQuery, so writes are committed first.
- SQL rewrites return the same results as SPEC.md's reference SQL with less work:
  - list pages pick their ids before the per-article subqueries run;
  - tag names are looked up by primary key;
  - look-up-then-act pairs are combined into one batch.
- Session-level settings on its own connections only: `plan_cache_mode=force_generic_plan`, `jit=off`, `max_parallel_workers_per_gather=0`.
- bcrypt cost 10 for every hash and every login, computed up to 4 at a time per thread for throughput. It is checked against libxcrypt by `bin/conduit --bcrypt-selftest`.
- Design notes, every optimization with its measured effect, and the dead ends are in the submission's README.

## Rules checklist
- Rules 2 and 3: Postgres at `$DATABASE_URL` only. At most 95 connections (default 4 per CPU). No schema, server or role changes; only session-level settings at connection startup.
- Rule 4: passes `test/run.sh`, 197/197.
- Rule 5: no caching across requests. Only connections, prepared statements and the HMAC key schedule are kept.
- Rule 6: each batch commits at its Sync before the response is sent. No `synchronous_commit` changes, no unlogged tables.
- Rule 7: bcrypt cost 10 on register and password change. Every login is verified against the stored hash. Every token's HS256 signature and `exp` are verified on every request.
- Rule 8: no hard-coded responses and no benchmark detection.
- Rule 11: `install.sh` installs `build-essential liburing-dev libcrypt-dev` from the Ubuntu 24.04 archive. `build.sh` is one `gcc` call. No downloads and no binaries committed.
- Rule 12: no kernel tuning and no CPU pinning; only in-process settings (thread counts, pool sizes).
- Only files under `submissions/c-iouring-tigokraft/` are changed.

## How it was checked
- `test/run.sh` 197/197 in each of these setups:
  - an Ubuntu 24.04 VM set up with `box/setup-box.sh`, on the dev and the full seed;
  - the same VM with the batch queue forced on every request;
  - a clean `ubuntu:24.04` container against the `postgres:18` image, mirroring this repo's CI: `install.sh` as root, then the tests as a non-root user.
- A differential test against `examples/go` on the full seed: 1,740+ read requests covering all list filters, deep offsets, the heaviest feeds and articles, both anonymous and logged in. JSON compared with sorted keys: 0 differences.
- Load tests with `bench/cmd/loadgen` on an i5-9500 VM. Postgres and the server had 4 cores, so the numbers are not comparable with the official box:
  - a 5-minute hold at 10,000 users with think time x0.1: 12.8k req/s, p95 458 ms, p99 485 ms, 0 errors;
  - 80,000 open connections: p99 10.6 ms, 0 errors.

title: Add Swift/Hummingbird submission
body:
## Submission

`submissions/swift-hummingbird-denizakya/` — RealWorld Conduit in **Swift 6.4.1** on **Hummingbird 2.28.0** with **postgres-nio 1.33.1**. **Front: nginx.**

## Verification

- Built in the official `swift:6.4.1-noble` container (Linux x86_64, release).
- Locally (macOS/arm64, dev seed): `test/run.sh` **197 steps, 197 passed** on a fresh DB copy.
- Load probes with `bench/cmd/loadgen` (server + Postgres 18 + loadgen on one MacBook, `-articles 10000`):

| users | throughput | p95 | p99 | errors | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 200 | 54 req/s | 3.6 ms | 5.7 ms | 0% | PASS |
| 1,000 | 267 req/s | 2.6 ms | 4.7 ms | 0% | PASS |
| 3,000 | 800 req/s | 1.8 ms | 2.9 ms | 0% | PASS |
| 10,000 | 2,644 req/s | 27.7 ms | 187 ms | 0% | PASS |

(20,000 users was attempted but the *load generator* collapsed — macOS ephemeral-port exhaustion — so it says nothing about the server.)

## Implementation notes

- One process; SwiftNIO event loop per core; bcrypt cost 10 runs off the event loops on a concurrent dispatch queue; Postgres pool `10 × cores` capped at 95 (`max_connections = 100`).
- Reference SQL verbatim; no caching across requests; HS256 signature and `exp` re-verified on every request; `sub` issued as a decimal string.
- **bcrypt**: vendored the OpenBSD C implementation that Vapor 4 ships (`Sources/CVaporBcrypt`, MIT) behind a thin Swift wrapper. Rationale: the standalone pure-Swift bcrypt packages on the Swift Package Index could not verify hashes produced by Go's `x/crypto/bcrypt` (the seed's format); this C implementation verifies them correctly.
- Hand-rolled JSON encoder (exact `null`s, RFC 3339 with exactly 3 fractional digits, lists omit `body`); hand-rolled compact JWS over swift-crypto's `HMAC<SHA256>`.
- HTTP/1.1 keep-alive with a 75 s idle timeout (outlives Nginx's 60 s upstream keep-alive); unknown routes return the RealWorld JSON error shape.
- All dependencies pinned exactly in `Package.swift` + `Package.resolved`; `install.sh` sha256-checks the official Swift 6.4.1 Ubuntu 24.04 tarball.

Only files under `submissions/swift-hummingbird-denizakya/` are touched.

title: Add a C# submission on Kestrel and Npgsql
body:
Adds `submissions/csharp-kestrel-xeonfx/`: Conduit on .NET 10, Kestrel and Npgsql. Front: direct.

Where the time goes:
- **Read groups.** Reads queue up, and loops (two per core, one connection each) send what has queued, up to 32, as one `NpgsqlBatch` with one Sync. Postgres starts and ends one implicit transaction and flushes once per group instead of once per statement. Read Committed still takes a fresh snapshot per statement. A failing statement fails only its own read, and the reads after it run again.
- **Group commit.** Writes queue up, and two writer loops commit up to 128 at a time in one transaction, so one WAL flush serves them all. A response is sent only after its commit. A failing write fails alone, and the writes before it commit together.
- One statement per request, generic plans, statements prepared once per connection, text columns written into the JSON from their UTF-8 bytes, Npgsql's SQL rewriting off.
- bcrypt (cost 10) in `Security/Bcrypt/`: my CodeFusion.Security.Bcrypt 1.1.0, copied from codefusion-dotnet and cut to what the server uses, with no NuGet package. Dedicated threads, up to five hashes interleaved per worker, each round XORing its round key in before the S-box result arrives. 12.3 ms per hash on the 8581C by the library's measurements, against 60 ms for BCrypt.Net-Next. New hashes are `$2b$`, and the seed's `$2a$` hashes verify. The rig results below were measured with the earlier bcrypt in this folder.
- Bounded queues for reads, writes and logins: past the limit a request gets a 503 with `Retry-After` at once instead of piling up. A lock or statement timeout is also a 503. An `Authorization` header that is present but empty is a 401.
- No spinning thread pool, server GC, a `switch` router, pooled response buffers, and a stats line every 10 s.

The submission's README has the details and numbers.

## Results

8-vCPU `c4-highcpu-8` (Xeon Platinum 8581C, 16 GB) set up with `box/setup-box.sh`, the load from two more `c4-highcpu-8` machines, full seed, think-scale 1. Each run: fresh database, 3 min warm-up, 60 s ramp, 60 s measured.

| Version | Most users passed | p95 / p99 there | CPU | Memory | Next step up |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| This version | **125,000** (the rig's maximum) | 192 / 231 ms | 98% | 4.8 GB | not reachable on this rig |
| Before the bcrypt change (205e743) | **125,000** (the rig's maximum) | 217 / 279 ms | 98% | 4.7 GB | not reachable on this rig |

Two load machines open about 64k connections each, so 125,000 is the most this rig can drive. Both versions passed 100,000, 110,000, 120,000 and 125,000 with no errors and used the same CPU per request: bcrypt is about 7% of the box at this load. At 125,000 Postgres uses 70 of the 98% CPU.

Earlier rig, one load machine and a target with two addresses (100,000 was its maximum):

| Version | Most users passed | p95 / p99 there | CPU | Memory | Next step up |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 205e743 | **100,000** (the rig's maximum) | 273 / 313 ms | 98% | 4.1 GB | not reachable on this rig |
| First version of this PR (b2a554c) | 80,000 | 59 / 149 ms | 96% | 4.2 GB | 100,000 fails: p95 1,198 ms, p99 1,880 ms |
| Go example | 30,000 | 8 / 15 ms | 84% | 2.7 GB | not tried |

The same commit passes more users on the newer rig, so compare rows only within a table.

## Testing

- `test/run.sh`: 197/197 on the full seed for this version.
- 207 xUnit tests against a real Postgres:
  - **Read groups:** grouping in one transaction, a failing read failing alone, a statement that fails after the row its read took, reads dropped when their client has gone, the queue limit, a broken connection, concurrent reads.
  - **Group commit:** failure isolation, deadlock retries, lock timeout, aborts.
  - **Favorite counts under races**, list pagination and caps, text round trips, auth headers.
  - **passwords** on the bcrypt in `Security/Bcrypt/`, against BCrypt.Net-Next for `$2a$`, `$2b$` and `$2y$` hashes, aborted calls and the 72-byte limit; a full bcrypt queue is a 503. Plus JWT and query-parsing properties (FsCheck).
- BenchmarkDotNet for bcrypt (1 to 5 lanes, against BCrypt.Net-Next), JWT, query parsing, JSON and database reads (`Benchmarks/DbBenchmarks.cs`).

title: feat(c): add C + io_uring + pipelined PostgreSQL submission (c-iouring-27bhd)
body:
## Summary

Adds `submissions/c-iouring-27bhd/` — a zero-framework C implementation of the Conduit API (SPEC.md) for the 8 vCPU / 16 GB PostgreSQL 18 box.

**Front: direct** (binds `0.0.0.0:80`; no Nginx).

Passes the conformance suite: `test/run.sh submissions/c-iouring-27bhd` → **197/197 steps, 0 failed**.

## Stack

| Piece | Version / details |
|---|---|
| Language | C11 (GCC 13+), `-O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto -fno-plt` |
| Network | Thread-per-core `io_uring` event loop, `SO_REUSEPORT`, `TCP_DEFER_ACCEPT`, `TCP_NODELAY` |
| Database | Raw PostgreSQL v3 wire protocol (`pg_wire.h`); `libpq` used only at startup for auth and `Parse` |
| Crypto | HMAC-SHA256 (precomputed key midstates); bcrypt cost 10 via `libxcrypt` `crypt_rn`, offloaded to a dedicated thread pool |
| JSON | In-place AVX2 string escaping, length-bounded wire parsing, zero-copy serialization |

## How it uses the cores

Eight worker threads pinned one per core (`pthread_setaffinity_np`), each with its own `io_uring` ring, its own set of accepted client sockets, and its own PostgreSQL connection. Listening sockets use `SO_REUSEPORT`.

## Key optimisations

- **One PostgreSQL round trip per endpoint.** List endpoints pipeline `[page][count]` under a single `Sync`. `favorite` pipelines the `INSERT`/`DELETE` with the read-back under one `Sync`, which sidesteps the data-modifying-CTE snapshot rule.
- **CTE fusions** for `update_article`, `delete_article`, `delete_comment` and `follow` (the 404/403 decision and the mutation happen in one statement). Article creation uses `currval(pg_get_serial_sequence('articles','id'))`, so the client never needs the server-generated id.
- **Literal fast-path statements** for the common `(limit, offset)` combinations, plus session-level `SET jit = off; SET plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan; SET TimeZone = 'UTC';`.
- **Bcrypt offload**: cost-10 hash/verify runs on dedicated `SCHED_BATCH` threads; the network loop is woken via an `eventfd` so it never blocks on a hash.
- **Zero-memmove response framing**: the status line and headers are written into a reserve directly in front of the body and transmitted as a single buffer.

## Rules

- **No cross-request caching** of any kind — no response, query-result, JWT-verification or bcrypt-result caches. Every request reads PostgreSQL while it is served.
- Writes are **committed before the response is queued** (pipelined `Sync`); `synchronous_commit` untouched.
- Real **bcrypt cost 10** and real **HS256** signature + `exp` verification on every request.
- No schema changes, no extra indexes/views/triggers; reads and writes only.

## Local load testing

Using `bench/cmd/loadgen` against the 2% dev seed with the load generator on the same host, this reached **64,000 concurrent virtual users at a 0.00% error rate** (p95 143 ms, p99 443 ms, ~1.1 GB RSS). Beyond that, single-host loopback port exhaustion stops the load generator, not the server. Official scoring is, of course, whatever the box measures on the full seed.

title: Add cpp-asio-c-hatton (C++20 / Boost.Asio / libpq pipeline)
body:
Adds `submissions/cpp-asio-c-hatton/`: C++20, Boost.Asio 1.83, libpq pipeline mode. **Front: direct.**

- Thread per core: each worker has its own `SO_REUSEPORT` listener and its own Postgres connections (16 in total on 8 cores). Requests are pipelined onto those connections with binary results, mostly one statement per request.
- Group commit for writes. Each response waits for its own commit, and a failed batch is retried one request at a time.
- List SQL picks the page's rows first and only then computes tags/counts/flags, so skipped OFFSET rows aren't decorated. Session-level `plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan` and `jit = off`. Results are identical to the reference SQL: a differential test (`tools/difftest.py`) had 0 mismatches in ~5,000 checks on the full seed.
- bcrypt at cost 10, computing up to 4 hashes interleaved on one thread. Output is bit-identical to libxcrypt, which handles anything outside ASCII passwords.
- `test/run.sh`: 197/197 on the dev seed, on the full seed, and from a clean Ubuntu 24.04 install.

Local numbers (Ryzen 7700X, server + Postgres pinned to 4 cores / 8 threads, full seed): about 46% of the Go example's total CPU at the same load, and ~35k req/s at p99 ≈ 20 ms vs ~13k for the Go example. Details are in the submission README.

title: Add rust-hyper-cknutson12 submission (Rust, hyper + tokio-postgres, Front: direct)
body:
Adds `submissions/rust-hyper-cknutson12/`: Rust (hyper 1 + tokio-postgres), **Front: direct**.

## What it does

- **One SQL statement per request.** Lists and the feed fold the capped count into the page query. Comments fold in the article lookup. Favorite, follow, comment and delete are data-modifying CTEs, and article create (with its tags) is a single statement, so it is still one transaction. The only exception is the rare `PUT /api/articles/:slug`.
- **Per-row subqueries only for returned rows.** The page is cut before tags, favorites count, favorited and following are computed, so rows skipped by OFFSET cost nothing. Tag names come from primary-key lookups.
- **The global count reads frozen pages.** It walks the primary key from the oldest end, so it stays an index-only scan with no heap fetches while new articles keep the newest pages changing.
- **Pipelined read connections, separate write connections.** Reads never queue behind a commit's WAL flush, and commits on different backends can share a flush.
- **Prepared statements with generic plans.** `plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan` and `jit = off` are set per session.
- **No framework on the app side.** Responses are written by hand, the allocator is mimalloc, and bcrypt runs behind a semaphore.

No caching of any kind. Every write is committed before its response. bcrypt cost 10 is used for every hash and every login, and every token's signature, `alg` and `exp` are checked on every request. The README has the details.

## Testing

- `test/run.sh`: **197/197** on a clean x86_64 Ubuntu 24.04 (`install.sh` as root, build and test as a normal user), and on arm64.
- Local load test (Docker on a laptop, full seed, server and Postgres sharing 8 vCPUs, `-think-scale 0.1`): at 5,000 VUs this submission had p95 5 ms and p99 51 ms, against 192 ms and 628 ms for the Go example on the same setup. It still passes at 7,000 VUs (~17k req/s). The README has the table; these are not box numbers.

One note for the Rust example: its `build.sh` sets `CARGO_HOME=$HOME/.cargo` without `/usr/local/cargo/bin` on `PATH`, so on a clean box cargo can't find `rustc` (exit 127). GitHub runners have rustup preinstalled in `~/.cargo/bin`, which hides this in CI. This submission's `build.sh` adds the PATH entry.
